questions.stem: In economics, demand for a commodity means the quantity that consumers are

options.text: willing and able to buy at a given price in a given period
in need of, whether or not they can pay for it
offered for sale by producers at a given price
able to buy only when prices are falling

questions.explanation: Demand requires both willingness and ability to pay, and it must be tied to a stated price and period. A desire without purchasing power is a mere want, not demand.

distractorRationale.b: Need without ability to pay is desire; it does not register in any market
distractorRationale.c: Quantity offered for sale is supply, not demand
distractorRationale.d: Demand exists at every price, high or low; only its size changes

questions.stem: A normal demand curve slopes downwards from left to right because

options.text: producers supply more as price rises
consumers buy more of a commodity as its price falls
the cost of production falls as output rises
government fixes prices below the market level

questions.explanation: The negative slope simply pictures the law of demand: a lower price raises real purchasing power and makes the good cheaper than its substitutes, so more is bought.

distractorRationale.a: That describes the upward-sloping supply curve
distractorRationale.c: Falling unit costs concern production, and would affect supply rather than demand
distractorRationale.d: Price control shifts attention to shortages; it does not explain the shape of the curve

questions.stem: From the demand schedule for tomatoes — ₦500: 10 baskets, ₦400: 20 baskets, ₦300: 35 baskets, ₦200: 55 baskets, ₦100: 80 baskets — by how many baskets does quantity demanded rise when the price falls from ₦400 to ₦200? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: At ₦400 buyers take 20 baskets and at ₦200 they take 55 baskets, so the rise is 55 − 20 = 35 baskets. Because the good's own price caused the change, this is an extension of demand along the same curve.

questions.stem: An increase in the minimum wage causes households to buy more beef. In terms of the demand curve for beef, this is shown by

options.text: a movement down along the existing demand curve
a shift of the whole demand curve to the right
a shift of the whole demand curve to the left
a movement up along the existing demand curve

questions.explanation: The price of beef has not changed; income has. Any non-price factor shifts the entire curve, and since beef is a normal good, higher income increases demand at every price, moving the curve rightward.

distractorRationale.a: Movements along the curve occur only when the good's own price changes
distractorRationale.c: A leftward shift would mean demand fell, which is what a fall in income would cause
distractorRationale.d: An upward movement along the curve would follow a rise in the price of beef itself

questions.stem: Cars and petrol are said to be in

options.text: competitive demand
composite demand
complementary demand
derived demand

questions.explanation: The two goods are used together and one is of little use without the other, so a rise in the price of petrol reduces the demand for cars. Goods related in this way are complements, also described as being in joint demand.

distractorRationale.a: Competitive demand applies to substitutes such as rice and spaghetti
distractorRationale.b: Composite demand applies to one good wanted for several different uses, such as maize
distractorRationale.d: Derived demand applies to a good wanted for what it helps produce, such as cement for houses

questions.stem: The demand for labour by a bakery is an example of

options.text: direct demand
derived demand
competitive demand
composite demand

questions.explanation: The bakery does not want bakers for their own sake; it wants them because bread is wanted. Demand for a factor of production is therefore derived from the demand for the product it makes.

distractorRationale.a: Direct demand is for goods that satisfy a want immediately, such as a loaf of bread itself
distractorRationale.c: Competitive demand concerns substitutes competing for the same buyer
distractorRationale.d: Composite demand concerns one commodity wanted for several different purposes

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates an exception to the law of demand?

options.text: A fall in the price of rice leads households to buy more rice
Sales of a luxury wristwatch rise after its price is doubled, because owning it now signals wealth
A rise in the price of beef causes buyers to switch to chicken
Demand for umbrellas rises during the rainy season

questions.explanation: Goods of ostentation, or Veblen goods, are bought partly because they are expensive, so quantity demanded can rise with price. That is a genuine reversal of the law of demand.

distractorRationale.a: This is the law of demand behaving exactly as predicted
distractorRationale.c: This is the substitution effect, which supports rather than contradicts the law
distractorRationale.d: A seasonal rise is a shift of the whole demand curve caused by a non-price factor, not an exception to the law

questions.stem: A fall in the price of a commodity causes an increase in demand for that commodity.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. A fall in the good's own price causes an extension of demand — a movement down along the same demand curve. An increase in demand means the whole curve shifts rightward, and only non-price factors such as income or taste can do that.

distractorRationale.a: This confuses movement along a curve with a shift of the curve, the most heavily penalised error in this topic

questions.stem: The law of demand states that, all else being equal, when the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded will:

options.text: decrease
increase
remain constant
fluctuate unpredictably

questions.explanation: According to the law of demand, there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded. When prices decrease, consumers are more likely to purchase larger quantities of the good.

distractorRationale.a: This option contradicts the law of demand.
distractorRationale.c: The quantity demanded does not remain constant when prices change.
distractorRationale.d: Price changes typically lead to predictable changes in quantity demanded.

questions.stem: If the price of oranges decreases from ₦200 to ₦150 and the quantity demanded increases from 30 to 50, this scenario illustrates:

options.text: a change in demand
a change in quantity demanded
an increase in supply
a decrease in supply

questions.explanation: This situation demonstrates a change in quantity demanded due to a price change, as consumers respond to the lower price by purchasing more oranges.

distractorRationale.a: A change in demand would involve factors other than price.
distractorRationale.c: This scenario does not involve supply changes.
distractorRationale.d: There is no indication of a decrease in supply.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a determinant of demand?

options.text: Consumer income
Consumer preferences
Price of related goods
Cost of production

questions.explanation: The cost of production affects supply, not demand. Determinants of demand include consumer income, preferences, and the prices of related goods.

distractorRationale.a: Consumer income directly influences demand levels.
distractorRationale.b: Consumer preferences impact how much of a good is demanded.
distractorRationale.c: The price of related goods can shift demand for a product.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations would likely lead to a decrease in the demand for a product?

options.text: An increase in consumer income
A successful advertising campaign
A rise in the price of a substitute good
A decrease in consumer preferences for the product

questions.explanation: A decrease in consumer preferences for a product will lead to lower demand, as fewer consumers want to purchase it regardless of price changes.

distractorRationale.a: Higher income typically increases demand for normal goods.
distractorRationale.c: An increase in the price of a substitute would likely increase demand for this product.

questions.stem: Which of the following examples best illustrates the concept of derived demand?

options.text: The demand for ice cream increases during summer
The demand for steel increases because of higher construction activity
The demand for luxury cars rises with higher income
The demand for bread decreases with a rise in its price

questions.explanation: Derived demand occurs when the demand for one good results from the demand for another good. In this case, the demand for steel is derived from the increased demand for construction.

distractorRationale.a: This example shows seasonal demand, not derived demand.
distractorRationale.c: This illustrates normal demand related to income, not derived demand.
distractorRationale.d: This is a direct relationship between price and demand, not derived.

questions.stem: A demand schedule is best described as:

options.text: A table showing the relationship between price and quantity supplied
A graphical representation of demand
A table showing the relationship between price and quantity demanded
A list of consumer preferences

questions.explanation: A demand schedule is a table that lists various prices of a good and the corresponding quantities demanded at those prices, illustrating the law of demand.

distractorRationale.a: This describes a supply schedule, not a demand schedule.
distractorRationale.b: A graphical representation is known as a demand curve.
distractorRationale.d: Consumer preferences are qualitative, not quantitative data like a demand schedule.

questions.stem: Which of the following would result in a rightward shift of the demand curve for a good?

options.text: A decrease in the price of the good
An increase in consumer income
A rise in the price of a substitute good
All of the above

questions.explanation: All listed factors can lead to an increase in demand, which is represented by a rightward shift of the demand curve. Lower prices, higher income, and higher substitute prices all encourage more purchasing.

distractorRationale.a: While a decrease in price increases quantity demanded, it does not shift the demand curve.
distractorRationale.b: Higher income increases demand for normal goods.
distractorRationale.c: Higher prices for substitutes lead consumers to buy more of this good.

questions.stem: An exception to the law of demand is observed in:

options.text: Giffen goods
Normal goods
Inferior goods
Complementary goods

questions.explanation: Giffen goods are a classic exception to the law of demand, where an increase in price leads to an increase in quantity demanded due to the income effect outweighing the substitution effect.

distractorRationale.b: Normal goods follow the law of demand.
distractorRationale.c: Inferior goods also follow the law of demand.
distractorRationale.d: Complementary goods typically follow the law of demand as well.

questions.stem: If the demand for a product increases due to a rise in consumer income, the product is classified as:

options.text: An inferior good
A normal good
A substitute good
A complementary good

questions.explanation: A normal good is one whose demand increases as consumer income rises. This is in contrast to inferior goods, which see a decrease in demand as income rises.

distractorRationale.a: Inferior goods experience decreased demand with increased income.
distractorRationale.c: Substitutes are related to demand changes due to price, not income.
distractorRationale.d: Complementary goods are linked to other products, not directly to income.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a movement along the demand curve?

options.text: A change in consumer income
A change in the price of the good
A change in consumer preferences
A change in the price of a substitute good

questions.explanation: A movement along the demand curve occurs when there is a change in the price of the good itself, resulting in a change in the quantity demanded.

distractorRationale.a: Changes in income shift the entire demand curve.
distractorRationale.c: Changes in preferences also shift the demand curve.
distractorRationale.d: Changes in substitute prices shift the demand curve, not cause movement along it.

questions.stem: The law of demand indicates that, ceteris paribus, when the price of a good increases, the quantity demanded will:

options.text: increase
decrease
remain the same
fluctuate

questions.explanation: According to the law of demand, there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded. As the price of a good rises, consumers tend to buy less of it, leading to a decrease in quantity demanded.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect because an increase in price typically leads to a decrease in quantity demanded.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as the law of demand specifies a change in quantity demanded with a price change.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect because price changes do not cause demand to fluctuate randomly; they lead to predictable changes in quantity demanded.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a change in demand?

options.text: A decrease in price leading to a lower quantity demanded
A shift of the demand curve to the left or right
A change in consumer preferences
An increase in quantity demanded due to a price drop

questions.explanation: A change in demand refers to a shift of the entire demand curve, which can occur due to factors such as changes in consumer income, preferences, or the prices of related goods. It is different from a change in quantity demanded, which is represented by a movement along the curve.

distractorRationale.a: This option describes a change in quantity demanded, not a change in demand.
distractorRationale.c: While changes in consumer preferences can lead to a change in demand, this option does not capture the definition of a change in demand itself.
distractorRationale.d: This option describes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift in the demand curve.

questions.stem: An increase in the price of a substitute good will likely result in:

options.text: An increase in the demand for the original good
A decrease in the demand for the original good
No change in the demand for the original good
A decrease in quantity demanded for the original good

questions.explanation: When the price of a substitute good increases, consumers may switch to the original good, leading to an increase in its demand. This reflects the relationship between substitutes in demand.

distractorRationale.b: This option is incorrect as it contradicts the expected behavior of consumers when substitute prices rise.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect because a change in the price of a substitute typically affects demand.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect since it confuses demand with quantity demanded, which is affected by price changes.

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios illustrates the concept of derived demand?

options.text: An increase in the demand for electric cars leading to more demand for batteries
A rise in the price of oranges causing a decrease in demand for apples
A decrease in the price of smartphones leading to increased demand for phone cases
A change in fashion trends affecting the demand for winter coats

questions.explanation: Derived demand occurs when the demand for one good results from the demand for another good. In this case, the demand for electric cars increases the demand for batteries, which are necessary for their production.

distractorRationale.b: This option illustrates a relationship between two goods but does not represent derived demand.
distractorRationale.c: This option shows a relationship between complementary goods, not derived demand.
distractorRationale.d: This option illustrates a change in demand due to fashion, not derived demand.

questions.stem: If a product is considered an inferior good, an increase in consumer income will likely lead to:

options.text: An increase in demand for the product
A decrease in demand for the product
No change in demand for the product
An increase in quantity demanded for the product

questions.explanation: Inferior goods are those for which demand decreases as consumer income increases. As people earn more, they tend to buy less of inferior goods and opt for higher-quality alternatives.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect because the definition of inferior goods states that demand decreases with increased income.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as it fails to recognize the relationship between income and demand for inferior goods.

A graphical representation of demand
A list of consumer preferences

questions.explanation: A demand schedule is a table that illustrates the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded by consumers at various price levels. It helps in understanding how demand changes with price.

distractorRationale.c: This option describes a demand curve, not a demand schedule.

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates the law of demand?

options.text: As the price of a luxury car decreases, more people choose to buy it
An increase in the price of bread leads to higher consumption of rice
As the price of a smartphone rises, fewer people are able to afford it
A rise in the price of gasoline results in increased demand for electric cars

questions.explanation: The law of demand states that when the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded increases, assuming all other factors remain constant. The scenario of the luxury car illustrates this principle effectively.

distractorRationale.b: This option illustrates the concept of substitutes, not the law of demand.
distractorRationale.c: This option describes a decrease in quantity demanded, which is a movement along the demand curve, not a change in demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a Giffen good?

options.text: Luxury watches
Staple foods like rice in a poor economy
High-end electronics
Designer clothing

questions.explanation: A Giffen good is a type of inferior good for which demand increases as the price rises, due to the income effect outweighing the substitution effect. Staple foods like rice can serve as Giffen goods in certain economic conditions.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect as luxury goods typically do not exhibit Giffen behavior.
distractorRationale.c: High-end electronics are not Giffen goods as they are generally not essential and have substitutes.
distractorRationale.d: Designer clothing does not fit the criteria for a Giffen good as it is not a necessity.

questions.stem: If a product's demand increases due to a change in consumer tastes, this is an example of:

options.text: A change in quantity demanded
A change in demand
Derived demand
Market equilibrium

questions.explanation: A change in consumer tastes can lead to a shift in the demand curve, indicating a change in demand rather than just a change in quantity demanded. This reflects the responsiveness of demand to consumer preferences.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect as it describes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift.
distractorRationale.c: This option does not apply as derived demand relates to the demand for goods based on the demand for other goods.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect because market equilibrium refers to the point where supply and demand meet, not a change in demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the concept of complementary goods?

options.text: Goods that are used together, such that an increase in demand for one leads to an increase in demand for the other
Goods that can replace each other in consumption
Goods that are unrelated in terms of consumer preference
Goods that are produced using the same resources

questions.explanation: Complementary goods are products that are consumed together. An increase in demand for one good typically leads to an increase in demand for its complement, as they enhance each other's utility.

distractorRationale.b: This option describes substitute goods, not complementary goods.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as complementary goods are related in consumption.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect because it does not accurately define complementary goods.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors would cause a leftward shift in the demand curve for a product?

options.text: A decrease in consumer income
An increase in the price of a substitute good
A decrease in the price of a complementary good
An increase in consumer preferences for the product

questions.explanation: A leftward shift in the demand curve indicates a decrease in demand at all price levels. A decrease in consumer income typically leads to a reduction in demand for normal goods, causing the demand curve to shift leftward.

distractorRationale.b: An increase in the price of a substitute good would likely increase demand for the product in question, shifting the demand curve rightward.
distractorRationale.c: A decrease in the price of a complementary good would generally increase demand for the product, resulting in a rightward shift.
distractorRationale.d: An increase in consumer preferences for the product would lead to an increase in demand, shifting the demand curve to the right.

questions.stem: What does the term 'quantity demanded' refer to?

options.text: The total amount of a good that consumers are willing to buy at a given price
The relationship between price and quantity demanded
The demand curve for a particular product
The maximum price consumers are willing to pay for a good

questions.explanation: Quantity demanded refers to the specific amount of a good that consumers are willing to purchase at a specific price, reflecting the law of demand.

distractorRationale.b: The relationship between price and quantity demanded is described by the demand curve, not quantity demanded itself.
distractorRationale.c: The demand curve illustrates demand, but quantity demanded is a specific point on that curve.
distractorRationale.d: The maximum price consumers are willing to pay is related to demand but does not define quantity demanded.

questions.stem: Which of the following types of goods would typically see an increase in demand when consumer incomes rise?

options.text: Inferior goods
Normal goods
Giffen goods
Substitute goods

questions.explanation: Normal goods see an increase in demand as consumer incomes rise, as consumers tend to purchase more of these goods when they have more income.

distractorRationale.a: Inferior goods experience a decrease in demand as incomes rise, as consumers shift to higher-quality alternatives.
distractorRationale.c: Giffen goods are a special case where demand increases despite a price rise, but they are not typically affected by income changes in the same way as normal goods.
distractorRationale.d: Substitute goods may see increased demand if the price of the original good rises, but they do not directly benefit from an increase in consumer income.

A graph representing consumer preferences
